question:
A 40-year-old man with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of intermittent fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. He has also had a nonproductive cough and a 3.6-kg (8-lb) weight loss in this period. He was treated for pneumocystis pneumonia 2 years ago. He has had skin lesions on his chest for 6 months. Five weeks ago, he went on a week-long hiking trip in Oregon. Current medications include efavirenz, tenofovir, and emtricitabine. He says he has had trouble adhering to his medication. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows oral thrush on his palate and a white, non-scrapable plaque on the left side of the tongue. There is axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. There are multiple violaceous plaques on the chest. Crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Abdominal examination shows mild, diffuse tenderness throughout the lower quadrants. The liver is palpated 2 to 3 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen is palpated 1 to 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL
Leukocyte count 4,800/mm3
CD4+ T-lymphocytes 44/mm3 (Normal ≥ 500 mm3)
Platelet count 258,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 137 mEq/L
Cl- 102 mEq/L
K+ 4.9 mEq/L
Alkaline phosphatase 202 U/L
One set of blood culture grows acid-fast organisms. A PPD skin test shows 4 mm of induration. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's condition?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: HIV infection -> low CD4+ T-lymphocytes -> increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections -> 80% CHAIN: AIDS -> immunocompromised state -> increased risk of fungal, bacterial, and viral infections -> 75% CHAIN: Pneumocystis pneumonia history -> previous opportunistic infection -> compromised immune system -> 70% CHAIN: Skin lesions on chest -> possible Kaposi sarcoma -> associated with HIV/AIDS -> 60% CHAIN: Weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea -> symptoms of systemic infection -> 70% CHAIN: Oral thrush, non-scrapable plaque on tongue -> signs of oral candidiasis -> common in immunocompromised individuals -> 80% CHAIN: Axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy -> lymph node involvement -> systemic infection -> 70% CHAIN: Violaceous plaques on chest -> possible Kaposi sarcoma -> common in HIV/AIDS patients -> 60% CHAIN: Crackles on chest auscultation -> pulmonary involvement -> 70% CHAIN: Liver and spleen palpation findings -> hepatosplenomegaly -> systemic infection -> 70% CHAIN: Blood culture grows acid-fast organisms -> likely mycobacterial infection -> 80% CHAIN: PPD skin test positive -> exposure to mycobacterium tuberculosis -> 90% CHAIN: Most appropriate pharmacotherapy for mycobacterial infection -> Rifampin and isoniazid -> standard treatment for tuberculosis -> 80%
analysis: The patient's presentation is concerning for disseminated histoplasmosis, given his history of AIDS, recent hiking trip to an endemic area, and the presence of skin lesions, oral thrush, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and pulmonary symptoms. The positive blood culture for acid-fast organisms is likely a result of a cross-reaction with Histoplasma antigen. Treatment of choice for disseminated histoplasmosis in an AIDS patient is with liposomal amphotericin B followed by itraconazole for maintenance therapy.
